Inaugurated 1 December 2002 by Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee

Living Museum

A Sacred Hill Transformed

Before this park, the hill was dense, untouched jungle. Today it stands as a living museum of Indian civilisation — a vision realised by the Mohan Shakti Trust, whose mission was to preserve and promote India's ancient Vedic traditions, spiritual teachings, and cultural values for generations to come.

Local artisans sculpted every murti by hand. The hills were sacred long before the park was built; the Trust simply made that sacredness visible to the world.

The Collection

108 Voices in Stone

Each murti stands 4–6 feet tall, sculpted by local artisans from the surrounding hills. They bring to life figures from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and the broader Vedic cosmos — gods, sages, warriors, and celestial beings.

Narasimha
Lion-man avatar of Vishnu — fierce protector
Durga
Warrior goddess in white stone — mid-battle
The Benevolent Goddess
Abhaya mudra — the gesture of fearlessness
The Praying Sage
Guru-shishya tradition in devotion
The Ragi
Saint musician — Bhakti tradition
Vedic Cosmos
The sacred number 108 — prayer and astronomy

The Visitor's Senses

What You Will
See, Hear & Feel

👁
See
108 hand-carved Vedic murtis arranged across 40 acres. A grand seven-horse chariot atop the main temple. Stone gods from the Ramayana and Mahabharata. Sculptures of extinct animals alongside ancient mythology.
🔔
Hear
Temple bells echoing across the hillside. Wind threading through ancient deodar trees. Birds in the surrounding jungle. Guides narrating forgotten stories of ancient India that no textbook carries.
✦
Feel
Awe at the scale of human devotion. A sense of living history beneath your feet. Curiosity as you identify deities — a quiet game of recognition that children and scholars share equally.
"

Heritage Park Guide Narration

The Guide's Words

Stones That Speak

A well-told story turns stone into experience. These are the phrases our guides share at the most significant murtis — where history, astronomy, and mythology converge.

"Look around you: every murti here was carved by local artisans. These hands shaped gods the way their ancestors shaped the valley — slowly, reverently, with the grain of the stone."

At the main sculptors' display

"Notice the number 108. It appears in Sanskrit prayers and in astronomy — it is not just decoration but also design. The Sun is 108 solar diameters from the Earth."

At the entrance courtyard

"Before this park, the hill was covered by dense jungle. The trust did not change the hill — they revealed it. Every step you take, the ground was already sacred."

Guide narration, heritage walk opening

"Can you identify which deity this is? The weapon in the hand, the vehicle below, the number of arms — each detail is language. Ancient India spoke in symbols, not sentences."

Interactive deity identification, all ages

Present & Future

Challenges &
Possibilities

Current Challenges

No audio guides or English signage — international visitors struggle to engage meaningfully with the stories behind each murti.

Several plaster sculptures show signs of weathering and need conservation attention.

Limited crowd management during peak seasons causes congestion near the main temple entrance.

Proposed Enhancements

QR codes at each murti linking to short video stories — bringing multilingual narration to every visitor's pocket.

Sunset and night illumination of the sculptures to create an atmospheric evening experience.

School heritage trail programmes and structured guided walks for students to connect with living Indian history.

Dedicated conservation plan for ageing sculptures and improved visitor flow management.
